title: Three-dimensional Deconvolution for Large-angle Illumination ADF-STEM Depth Sectioning
content: To fully understand material properties, it is crucial to determine the three-dimensional spatial distribution of point defects such as vacancies, interstitials, anti-sites, impurities, and their complexes. Since such defects are locally distributed in all three dimensions, high spatial resolution is required. With the development of aberration correctors, the spatial resolution of scanning transmission electron microscopy (STEM) has significantly improved, achieving a resolution of 40.5 pm in recent years [1]. Therefore, STEM imaging is a promising technique for determining the spatial distributions of point defects. However, such high spatial resolution is limited to the lateral direction, while the resolution along the remaining dimension, depth, is still typically several nanometers. Recently, a depth resolution of ±0.9 Å has been achieved by combining large-angle illumination annular dark-field (ADF)-STEM depth sectioning with statistical analysis of the intensity profiles, enabling the observation of atomistic defects on the oxide surface with atomic resolution [2]. However, the method is only applicable to the analysis of crystalline surfaces, and it is still a major challenge to perform 3D characterization in the bulk even with large-angle illumination STEM [3]. ADF-STEM imaging can be considered as an incoherent imaging, where the recorded intensity I(r) is represented as a 3D convolution between a probe function P(r) and an object function O(r) [4]:
